query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A pre-applied thin hafnium surface coating on high-entropy boride components will improve resistance to molten‐aluminum corrosion by forming a dense protective HfO2 scale and a graded interfacial HfZr transitional layer during hot-dip plating, with the process further enhanced by the sluggish diffusion inherent to multi-principal-element borides.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based (or high-entropy boride) component with an unmodified surface, as typically used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin hafnium coating via a hot-press sintering process onto the boride component prior to exposure to molten aluminum.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum under standard hot-dip plating conditions at the service temperature in an air-containing environment where reactive oxygen is present to stabilize the protective oxide layer.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an interfacial HfZr transition layer and a dense, adherent HfO2 scale on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure to molten aluminum, the hafnium coating reacts with available oxygen to form a stable HfO2 barrier, while interdiffusion with substrate elements forms a graded interfacial layer; this process is governed by sluggish diffusion inherent to high-entropy systems.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated boride components, the Hf-coated components will exhibit a lower corrosion rate and reduced oxide spallation, resulting in improved structural integrity and longer service life in molten-aluminum environments.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components without any surface modification or coating.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected under continuous hot-dip process conditions where the coating remains dense and defect-free; if the coating is too thin, non-uniform, or damaged during processing, the benefit may be lost.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of corrosion resistance improvement is not precisely known and may depend on the coating thickness, uniformity, and specific processing conditions. Long-term durability under thermal cycling remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy boride samples: one set with the proposed hafnium coating applied by hot-press sintering and one set left uncoated. Subject both sets to identical molten-aluminum immersion experiments simulating the hot-dip process conditions (temperature maintained around 700 °C in air for a fixed period). Post-exposure, evaluate the corrosion damage, weight gain, oxide layer adhesion, and microstructural integrity using SEM, EDS, and XRD.
measurements: Weight change per unit area (corrosion rate)
Oxide scale thickness and continuity measured by SEM
Phase identification of the protective oxide (e.g., HfO2) using XRD
Quantitative analysis of spallation or damage area
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20% lower corrosion rate and oxide spallation area) compared to the uncoated baseline under identical testing conditions, or if the protective oxide scale is not well formed on the coated samples, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application.
